L547: # About Emergency Access
L548: 
L549: Emergency access lets you prepare for the unexpected by appointing trusted emergency contacts who can request access to your Bitwarden vault if needed. Trusted emergency contacts can be granted either view or takeover access, giving you control over what they can do if they ever need to step in:
L550: 
L551:   * View: When an emergency access request is granted, this user is granted view/read access to all items in your individual vault, including login items' passwords and attachments.
L552:   * Takeover: When an emergency access request is granted, this user must create a master password for permanent read/write access to your vault. This will replace your previous master password and remove any 【29†two-step login methods】 that were previously set up.
L553: ## Set up and use emergency access
L554: 
L555: There are a few steps to grant someone emergency access to an account:
L556: 
L557:   1. The account holder 【38†adds a trusted contact】 for their account before an emergency arises.
L558: 
L559:   2. When needed, the trusted contact 【338†requests access】 to the account.
L560: 
L561:   3. The 【339†request is approved】 by the account holder or after the wait time expires.
L562: 
L563:   4. The 【340†trusted contact accesses the account】.
L564:   5. (Optional) The account holder 【341†revokes the trusted contact's access】 to their account.
L565: ## Who can use emergency access
L566: 
L567: 【38†Adding a trusted contact】 for emergency access is available to premium users, including members of paid organizations (Families, Teams, and Enterprise). If your organization turned on the 【342†Automatic confirmation policy】, emergency access is not available for your account.
L568: Anyone with a free or premium Bitwarden account on the same 【318†Bitwarden server】 can be designated as a trusted emergency contact. There is no limit to the number of trusted emergency contacts a premium user can have.
L569: 
L570: tip
L571: 
L572: If you're an organization administrator, 【162†account recovery】 may be a better fit for managing employee account access during offboarding or succession planning.
L573: ## How it works
L574: 
L575: note
L576: 
L577: The following information references encryption key names and processes that are discussed in 【343†hashing, key derivation, and encryption】. Consider reading those details first.
L578: 
L579: Emergency access uses public key exchange and encryption/decryption to allow users to give a trusted emergency contact permission to access vault data in a zero-knowledge encryption environment:
L580:   1. A Bitwarden user (the grantor) invites another Bitwarden user to become a trusted emergency contact (the grantee). The invitation specifies a user access level, includes a request for the grantee's RSA Public Key, and is valid for only five days.
L581: 
L582:   2. Grantee is notified of the invitation via email and accepts the invitation to become a trusted emergency contact. On acceptance, the grantee's RSA Public Key is stored with the user record.
L583:   3. Grantor is notified of the invitation's acceptance via email and confirms the grantee as their trusted emergency contact. On confirmation, the grantor's User Symmetric Key is encrypted using the grantee's RSA Public Key and stored with the invitation. Grantee is notified of confirmation.
L584: 
L585:   4. An emergency occurs, resulting in grantee requiring access to grantor's vault. Grantee submits a request for emergency access.
L586:   5. Grantor is notified of the request via email. The grantor may manually approve the request at any time, otherwise the request is bound by a grantor-specified wait time. When the request is approved or the wait time lapses, the Public Key-encrypted User Symmetric Key is delivered to the grantee for decryption with the grantee's RSA Private Key.
L587: Alternatively, the grantor may reject the request, which will prevent the grantee gaining access as described in the next step. Rejecting a request will not remove the grantee from being a trusted emergency contact or prevent them from making access requests in the future.
L588:   6. Depending on the specified user access level, the grantee will either:
L589: 
L590:      * View: Obtain view/read access to items in the grantor's vault.
L591: 
L592:      * Takeover: Be asked to create a new master password for the grantor's vault.
L593: ## Next steps
L594: 
L595:   * 【38†Add trusted emergency contacts】 to your account.
L596: 
L597:   * Share with your trusted contacts 【338†how to request access】, should the need arise.
L598: 
L599:   * Learn how to 【344†handle emergency access requests】 to your account.

L109: ## Your credentials remain encrypted
L110: 
L111: Even when you approve access to an account, your AI agents don’t see your passwords. Everything in your vault remains protected.
L112: 
L113: 【6†Try 1Password free】
L114: 
L115: ## Frequently asked questions
L116: ### Will an AI agent see my passwords?
L117: No. 1Password for Agents lets AI agents sign in without receiving or seeing the credential. When an agent reaches a sign-in form, it uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password. The person sees which credential it needs and why, and then chooses whether to approve the request. That approval happens on the person’s own device, confirming that the permission came from them. 1Password then fills it directly into the sign-in form instead of sending it to the agent.
L118: Once signed in, the agent continues the task while the password stays protected in 1Password.
L119: ### Can an AI agent access my whole vault?
L120: 
L121: No. Connecting an agent does not give it access to everything in your vault. It requests a login for a task, and you decide whether to approve that request. The agent can’t see the credentials, and your other saved passwords in your vault remain protected by end-to-end encryption.
L122: ### Do I control which login an agent uses?
L123: 
L124: Yes. You review the access request and can approve or deny it. If more than one saved login matches, you can choose which one 1Password uses. How often you are asked to approve access may vary by integration.
L125: ### How does Agentic Autofill work?
L126: 
L127: Agentic Autofill helps a supported agent sign in through a browser without handling the password itself. When the agent requests a login and you approve it, 1Password fills the password or one-time code into the sign-in page so the agent can continue its task.
L128: ### What can an agent do after it signs in?
L129: 
L130: An agent may be able to see information or take actions within the signed-in account. Its behavior there depends on the agent and the website. Review the task and the account before approving access.
L131: ### Which AI agents work with 1Password?
L132: 
L133: 1Password for Agents works with supported personal and coding agent integrations, rather than every AI tool. Check the 【7†integration cards】 on this page for available and coming-soon connections. Features may vary by agent.
L134: ### Who can use 1Password for Agents?
L135: 
L136: The new personal agent integrations are being introduced for 1Password Individual and Families accounts. Availability and setup requirements can vary by integration, region, device, and sign-in method. Check each integration’s details before getting started.
L137: 
L138: ### Do I have to use an AI agent with 1Password?
L139: 
L140: No. These integrations are optional. If you do not connect an agent, you can continue using 1Password as you do today.

L154: ## When there is no recovery path
L155: 
L156: Not every provider documents rotation. If the guide has no recovery section:
L157:   1. Stop. Do not re-run signup.
L158:   2. Check the provider's dashboard or account settings for a key reset, using the account reference from the receipt.
L159:   3. Ask the human owner to act in the provider's UI, since the account is attributed to them.
L160:   4. Contact the provider's support or security contact, which the discovery document or the guide should name.
L161:   5. If the provider has no path at all, the credential is gone. The account still exists and the human is still accountable for it; plan to replace the integration or the account deliberately, not by looping signup.
L162: ## Rotation and revocation
L163: 
L164: Rotate a provider credential when it may have leaked, when the agent is being retired, or on the provider's schedule. Rotation happens at the provider, with the provider's endpoint or dashboard.
L165: Revoking the agent in the broker does not rotate anything at the provider. Revocation stops new assertions and further identity and inbox calls; it does not touch credentials the agent already stored or accounts it already created. If you revoke because of a suspected compromise, rotate the provider credentials as a separate step, then review the ledger and inbox for unexpected activity.
L166: ## What the human should know
L167: 
L168: The human owner is accountable for the account the agent created, and can read the agent's inbox. Tell them, in plain terms: which provider, which account reference, where the credential is stored, and what the recovery path is. Do not send the credential itself through the inbox or the transcript.

L109: ## Advanced Permissions security model
L110: 
L111: Advanced Permissions are enforced onchain through 【29†Smart Accounts Kit's Smart Contracts†docs.metamask.io】. Here's what that means in practice:
L112: 
L113:   * Scoped by design: Each permission defines exactly what the session account can access: asset, amount, time window, and transfer type. The Delegation Framework's caveat enforcers reject any execution that falls outside scope.
L114:   * Human-readable approval: MetaMask displays a rich confirmation UI showing the full permission parameters before the user grants anything.
L115: 
L116:   * User-adjustable: If your permission request sets isAdjustmentAllowed: true, users can modify the parameters (e.g., reduce the amount or shorten the duration) before approving.
L117: 
L118:   * Revocable: Users can revoke any active permission at any time through MetaMask's Dapp connections option.
L119:   * Session accounts don't hold funds: Execution happens via delegation redemption from the user's Smart Account. The session account is a signing key, not a custody point.
L120: #### Ready to build? Get started with 【24†Advanced Permissions†docs.metamask.io】 in the Smart Accounts Kit today.
